item.title: SAP security advisory – October 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1030)
Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: Microsoft security advisory – October 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1038)
Palo Alto Networks security advisory (AV26-1041) - Update 1
OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
item.description:
Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices.

A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems.

Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL).

“PQC [post-quantum cryptography] migration in healthcare is not just about data confidentiality, but also patient safety,” the Forescout researchers say in their report, which examined over 2.5 million devices across more than 50 organizations. “Cryptography protects commands sent to medical devices, telemetry received from those devices for diagnostic purposes, medication orders, and other sensitive interactions. Quantum threats include unauthorized remote access by exploiting public keys for authentication, tampering with device-to-device communication by decrypting traffic, and sophisticated malware exploiting firmware integrity signatures.”

While upgrading to PQC is relatively straightforward for live servers, where a standardized PQC algorithm can be implemented as a library package upgrade and configuration change, embedded devices such as those used in healthcare need full firmware updates from their manufacturers. Moreover, those upgrades must maintain backwards compatibility with other systems that might not be upgraded at the same time, and in the case of certified devices, they might require re-certification.

This issue goes beyond healthcare to include industrial installations or anywhere OT or IoT devices handle sensitive or business-critical data.

Last month, the G7 Cybersecurity Working Group urged governments and organizations to begin migrating to PQC as soon as possible, calling for action across all sectors. The group warned that the transition will be lengthy and that organizations should prepare before quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptography become available.

Daniel dos Santos, VP of research at Forescout, tells CSO that while government bodies have issued orders and advisories with different expectations for PQC readiness, they all tend to converge on a 2030 timeline, which is when experts expect quantum computers might be capable of breaking existing encryption algorithms.

For industries such as healthcare, however, the HNDL threat collapses that quantum-readiness timeline completely.

Patient data travels beyond the medical device

Protecting patient information requires securing the entire communication chain, from the equipment that generates the data to the IT systems that store it and the applications that make it available to doctors and patients. That includes, for example, a CT scanner that sends images to a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), images that can later be transferred between hospitals, cloud services, and external radiology providers, requiring quantum-resistant protection on each transfer to maintain long-term confidentiality.

Laboratory results and prescription records follow similar routes. Electronic prescribing services exchange medication information between providers and pharmacies, including records of controlled substances and treatment for chronic diseases. Attackers can potentially intercept and siphon that data at different points in the chain: at the device level, from an internal network, through a compromised edge router or firewall, or even at the telecom operator’s level.

The platforms that store and exchange patient records are often accessible directly from the internet as well. In a Shodan search, Forescout identified more than 5,500 internet-exposed instances of medical information systems, with electronic medical record platforms accounting for 46% of those instances and PACS accounting for 40%.

Only 36% of PACS, 33% of electronic medical record systems, and 13% of laboratory information management systems had support for TLS 1.3, the only version of the protocol that supports ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), a quantum-resistant key encapsulation standard published by NIST. However, the presence of TLS 1.3 does not demonstrate that a connection uses quantum-resistant cryptography, because the connecting client might negotiate a different algorithm.

Furthermore, in a previous study published in June, Forescout found that only 11.8% of SSH servers on the internet are PQC-capable, a number that falls to 3% when looking only at Dropbear, an SSH server commonly used on embedded devices. Inside enterprise networks, 50% of IT devices use OpenSSH versions that support PQC, but only 28% of IoT, 16% of OT, and 6% of IoMT devices use the same versions.

“Specialized devices are unlikely to be fully migrated this decade if we keep going at the current pace, delaying broader PQC migration efforts and quantum readiness,” the researchers concluded. “Unfortunately, medical devices are among those with the lowest adoption rates and the hardest challenges for adopting PQC.”

Challenges extend beyond healthcare

Changing cryptography on equipment used for patient care or industrial operations is completely dependent on the device vendor. Dos Santos says modifying the device filesystem independently, even when it can be done, jeopardizes certification, maintenance, and support, and any communication protocol changes need to preserve connections to other equipment. The same problem exists for devices in chemical plants, electricity networks, water treatment facilities, and factory floors.

Some medical and industrial equipment already runs on Linux, which could in theory make adopting PQC easier, dos Santos says. However, he has seen little discussion of PQC adoption or roadmaps among OT vendors.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) described in its October 2024 OT guidance how changes to equipment controlling heavy machinery or combustible materials can require extensive safety testing. For medical devices, the regulatory implications depend on the changes made to the device. The US Food and Drug Administration’s February 2026 cybersecurity guidance says changes to authentication or encryption algorithms may require a new premarket submission.

Concerns about legacy equipment and PQC extend across sectors. In a Certes survey of 200 IT and security professionals engaged with quantum-related risks at large US and UK organizations published in May, 78% of respondents rated the potential quantum threat to legacy environments as very high. For edge and IoT equipment, including industrial and medical devices, ATMs, and vehicles, 43% rated the threat as very high and another 31% as significant.

Some devices will need alternative solutions

Healthcare information, financial records, and trade secrets, such as code and industrial designs, can remain sensitive years after transmission. But not all data exchanged between devices has the same confidentiality requirements or operational relevance over time.

“What’s missing from the policy conversation is a differentiated threat and risk assessment framework — one that accounts for data lifetime and sensitivity decay rate, device class, computational constraints, and realistic adversary capability timelines,” Sharon Hagi, CSO at IoT cybersecurity firm Finite State, told CSO in June after France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, outlined plans to introduce PQC requirements for product qualification starting in 2027.

“The quantum threat is not uniformly distributed across the cryptographic stack,” Hagi said. “Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA and ECC. It does not break AES-256 or SHA-3 in any operationally practical sense — Grover’s provides at most a quadratic speedup, and the effective security margins of properly sized symmetric primitives still holds for most uses. Architectures that rely on symmetric encryption with out-of-band or pre-provisioned key distribution remain meaningful options for resource-constrained embedded devices where NIST PQC algorithms (e.g. ML-KEM, ML-DSA) impose non-trivial compute, bandwidth, and memory costs.”

This means vendors will have to weigh carefully on which devices it’s even viable due to hardware limitations to deploy new PQC algorithms. In some cases, end-users might have to come up with alternatives, such as isolating those devices and routing traffic to and from them through other gateway devices that can apply PQC.

This is the approach that users should start taking before vendors decide to release firmware upgrades, dos Santos says. For example, internet-facing websites and portals should already be configured to use TLS 1.3 as all modern browsers support it. For remote management and file transfers over the internet, deploy gateways that support protocols with quantum-resistant cryptography.

A hospital could use a gateway to protect an image transfer to an external radiology provider. The hospital would still need to assess the connection from the scanner or image archive to that gateway and maybe isolate them on their own network segment with no direct internet access.

“But at least for the external part, you’re reducing risk, right?” dos Santos says.

But PQC support at one endpoint is effective only if the other endpoint can also negotiate the same algorithm, and manufacturers are reporting difficulty meeting interoperability goals. Thales’s September Manufacturing Data Threat Report, based on 417 respondents in 20 countries, revealed that 30% were behind on their post-quantum interoperability objectives.

“For the end users, the main thing to be doing right now is the inventory of devices and data together,” dos Santos said. “Devices, data, and communication.”

The resulting map should identify which transfers already have compatible protection, which depend on an upgrade, and where a gateway could protect an external connection.

For healthcare, Forescout recommends prioritizing patient portals, external APIs, partner exchanges, and other internet-facing connections, then updating cryptographic libraries and firmware where feasible. For equipment that cannot be upgraded, its healthcare report recommends assessing gateways and isolation measures, obtaining vendor roadmaps, and planning replacement when manufacturers have no viable migration path.

Dos Santos says vendors supplying equipment with multiyear service should have a roadmap for PQC communications even when their current firmware does not support it. Operators need to know when that support will arrive, which connections it will protect, and whether it requires new hardware. For equipment expected to remain in service for years, those answers need to inform purchasing and support agreements, alongside a replacement plan if a vendor cannot deliver an upgrade.

The G7 call to action urges organizations to integrate quantum-safe replacements into normal equipment renewal schedules and the US Office of Management and Budget’s June guidance directs federal agencies to incorporate PQC upgrades into hardware refreshes and prioritize replacing or decommissioning equipment that cannot support PQC or hybrid cryptography.

item.title: When defrost becomes sabotage: 3 OT lessons from France’s supermarket attack
item.description:
On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables.

Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000. Its chief executive, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that the cold chain held in most of them. Only a minority reacted too slowly and lost stock, and he credited store staff and refrigeration contractors for the difference. Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw away everything. A second wave followed in the night of 12 to 13 October, this time also reaching stores with Dixell controllers.

Similar controllers, similar night, very different mornings. That gap is the part of this story an operator can act on. CSO has already reported which systems were hit and what CERT-FR wants done with them. Nobody has claimed responsibility and no ransom demand has surfaced, which Reuters reports has puzzled investigators; whoever did this wanted spoiled food, not money, or has not said what they wanted yet. Neither CERT-FR nor Danfoss has said how the attackers got in: exposed management interfaces, known flaws and stolen contractor credentials are all still on the table. The three lessons that follow do not depend on either answer.

Your refrigeration contractor is your perimeter

Schelcher made a remark that deserves more attention than the temperature figures: Coopérative U stores do not buy from Danfoss. They buy from refrigeration contractors, who supply the controller, configure it and keep remote access to it so they can adjust setpoints without driving to the store. E.Leclerc told AFP that the attack reached its stores through one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers. The controller’s embedded web server exists for exactly this purpose, and the contractor’s performance guarantees usually depend on the data feed it provides.

Danfoss has seen this before. Its own technical newsletter from October 2025 records attacks on the AK-SM 800 in 2022: 16 Russian supermarkets and 40 Israeli stores. All 40 Israeli sites, the newsletter notes, lacked proper firewall or VPN protection. Four years later the same model, end-of-life since May 2021, was still on the internet in France.

The pattern is familiar from industrial sites. The party who decides whether a controller is exposed is not the party who eats the loss when it is. The contractor wants a browser and a public IP address because it turns a Sunday-night callout into a two-minute job. The store carries the inventory. A standard maintenance contract rarely makes that trade-off visible to the person signing it.

How deep the dependency runs shows in a sentence I have not seen in a national advisory before. CERT-FR’s alert, updated on 16 October, tells operators to check their insurance terms before cutting the internet link to the refrigeration contractor. The data feed is contractual, and depending on the agreement, cutting it can touch monitoring obligations or policy conditions. And the insurance side is bleak anyway: brokers and underwriters told Reuters that cyber policies typically exclude physical loss, so the spoiled stock is unlikely to be covered. Intermarché told AFP its insurance does not cover the incident.

So, the first question: who can log into your refrigeration controllers today, and over what path? Store network, contractor VPN, a cellular router the contractor installed years ago, a port forward on the store router? If answering requires calling the contractor, you do not control that perimeter. You rent it.

The lesson is a contract clause, not a firewall rule. The maintenance agreement should name every remote path into the equipment and forbid any other; require access through your gateway or VPN with accounts tied to named technicians; give you the logs; oblige the contractor to tell you when a controller leaves vendor support or a vulnerability is published; and let you revoke access without losing the cold chain. Cold-case controllers run for decades. The contract that pays for their maintenance rarely says any of this. After France, it should.

Defrost is a feature. Treat the command as the event

Whatever got the attackers in, the damage itself came from ordinary refrigeration functions. Defrost is a built-in cycle on every refrigeration controller, and in the second wave the setpoints were reportedly pushed to values no case can reach. Many controllers also offer a setting that suppresses temperature alarms during defrost and for a delay afterwards, so that scheduled cycles do not page anyone at 3 a.m. That is a sensible configuration. It is also exactly what makes a forced defrost quiet. Whether it played a role in France has not been established, and Coopérative U’s experience shows that alarms did reach people in most of its stores.

The structure is the same as in the Minnesota water attacks in July: intended functionality, used by the wrong person at the wrong time. A temperature alarm is a process control. It tells you the product is getting warm. It cannot tell you that the command which made it warm came from someone who should not have been logged in.

The signal worth alarming on is an unexpected mode or setpoint change outside a maintenance window, and it gets louder when several circuits move at once or several stores that share a contractor move in the same hour. CERT-FR’s updated alert now tells operators to review their defrost schedules specifically. That is the right instinct: look at the configuration, not just the thermometer.

Not every controller can export that event, least of all the models that were hit. Where it cannot, an independent temperature logger that does not depend on the controller catches the consequence early. Either way, someone has to receive the alert, understand it and have the authority to act. At 3 a.m. that chain runs from a store employee to an external technician to a central operations desk, and if nobody has written down who calls whom, the minutes go to finding out. In the second wave, a refrigeration technician in the Gironde told Le Monde that his teams reached a store near Bordeaux in time, and nothing had to be thrown away. Schelcher’s minority lost their stock because they could not respond fast enough. One factor clearly separated the two groups: time from first actionable warning to intervention.

The lesson, concretely: an alert on any remote setpoint or mode change that no technician has announced, weighted by time of day and by how many circuits move together, raised by the controller where it can and by the contractor’s monitoring platform where it cannot, since the contractor is the only party that sees all its stores at once. A temperature logger that does not share the controller’s network, as the second opinion. A written call chain for 3 a.m. with names, not roles. And a drill: have the contractor change a setpoint on a test circuit at night and measure how many minutes pass before someone with authority has it reversed. That number is the one to report to the board.

An unsupported controller is a budget line, not a patch ticket

Claroty’s Team82 published three flaws in the current model, the AK-SM 800A, in August, all fixed in firmware 4.3.1 or earlier, and counted 2,765 of its management interfaces reachable from the internet. Nobody has linked those flaws to the attack. Danfoss says most affected units were the older AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355, with some 800A units on outdated firmware.

For the older models, there is nothing to patch. Danfoss ended updates for the AK-SM 800 in May 2021 and for the AK-SC 355 in 2016. CERT-FR therefore does not lead with patching. It tells operators to take every AK-SM, AK-SC and XWEB controller off the public internet, restore access only through a VPN or protected network, and for compromised Danfoss units, restart, or failing that, factory-reset, and reconfigure before returning them to service. It adds a warning that reads like a prediction: a reset alone removes persistence but leaves the device just as vulnerable, and the campaign is probably still running.

The sequence is the one I argued for when CISA asked operators to harden Siemens S7 PLCs: exposure first, firmware second, replacement third. In practice, that means a list of every refrigeration controller by model, firmware and vendor support status by the end of this week; a management interface on a public IP address taken off it the same day; current firmware on everything the vendor still supports; and for everything it does not, a replacement date with a budget line and a name next to it. An aging controller may still do its job perfectly well, and replacing it costs money, engineering time and downtime, so without an owner the decision slides. The security team can document the risk. Someone on the commercial side has to accept it or fund the replacement, and after Reuters’ insurance round-up, that person should know they are also accepting the stock.

Which brings the story back to the two groups of stores. Nobody has shown that firmware or hardware explains which stores kept their stock. What is documented is that a warning reached someone who could act before the cold chain gave way. That is an operational capability, and it can be tested long before an attacker tests it for you. Sekoia told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium saw cases too, and the same controller families run cold storage in warehouses and pharmaceutical distribution, maintained by the same kind of contractor. So, before the week is out, do two things. Search Shodan or Censys for your own refrigeration management interfaces, because someone else already has. Then call the contractor and ask one question: when you log into our sites, how do you get there? If the answer is a public IP address and a password, with nothing in between, you have found your incident. It just hasn’t happened yet.

item.title: AL26-024 - Critical vulnerabilities affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway – CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 – Update 2
UK FCA exec wants to require disclosure of ‘significant AI failures and near-misses’
item.description:
When UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Data Officer Jessica Rusu gave a speech on Monday advocating that UK companies be required to report “significant AI failures and near-misses,” she added to the drumbeat of demands for some kind of regulatory control over enterprise AI deployments. 

But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency.

Rusu, speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience.

“Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too,” Rusu said. “It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress, or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.”

She added, “the FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators, and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.”

One of the questions that came out of the speech is what precisely was meant by “significant AI failures and near-misses.” Questions to FCA to clarify their terminology were not answered by publication time.

AI failure vs near miss

But Pieter Arntz, a malware intelligence researcher at security firm Malwarebytes, offered his own take on what those terms likely mean.

“A significant AI failure is one with serious consequences, not simply an incorrect answer. In financial services, that could mean an AI system authorizing substantial fraudulent payments, exposing sensitive customer information, denying customers access to essential financial services, or triggering transactions that threaten market integrity,” Arntz said. “The test should be the scale and severity of the impact, rather than whether the failure looks technically dramatic.”

On the other hand, he added, “An AI near-miss is an event that could realistically have caused serious harm, but was caught before that harm occurred. For example, an AI agent might attempt an unauthorized transfer that a separate approval control blocks, or a prompt-injection attack might induce it to disclose sensitive information, only for an outbound security control to stop the disclosure.”

However, Arntz warned of the risk to Rusu’s approach, should the final penalties be underwhelming. “There is a risk of this becoming a paper tiger if compliance amounts to filing a report and absorbing a predictable fine,” he said. 

Warnings from multiple directions

UK-based Gartner VP analyst Nader Henein said he is skeptical about the significance of the FCA’s proposal, in part because so many UK enterprises already have to comply with EU regulations, which have started asking companies to make such disclosures.

“Financial watchdogs including the Bank of England (BoE), the UAE Central Bank, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have all issued warnings,” he said. “A few months ago, the European central banks, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, escalated the cyber risk assessment level associated with frontier models to ‘severe,’ warning that simultaneous cyber incidents could impact the financial sector. They acknowledged that AI-driven cyber incidents now threaten core financial sector stability.”

Henein said that he is especially skeptical that meaningful changes will occur in the financial sector.

“Financial institutions tend to heed the warnings of the regulator that decides whether they can continue to operate, but without clear laws, regulatory oversight, and the obligatory fines, these disjointed statements are not likely to make a difference,” he said. 

Could ‘incentivize the wrong behavior’

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, added that one risk of this increased visibility requirement is that it could inadvertently incentivize the wrong behavior. 

“A bank with good monitoring may catch hundreds of attempts by AI agents to act outside their authority,” he said. “A bank with poor monitoring may report zero, because it never saw them. On paper, the safer bank looks worse. A model failing a red-team test is the test working, not a regulatory incident.”

However, Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, said that the near-miss approach has the strongest potential to change the conversation.

“I love the near-miss idea. It is the most important thing in the speech. It is the part financial firms are least ready for,” he said. 

But, he stressed, “[Rusu] also warns about reliance on a single model. An outage at one AI supplier that takes down a customer service channel counts, too.”

Another concern about reliance on a specific model is the ever-present risk that an AI vendor could change the model without telling all of its customers. 

“A model can pass testing in March and misbehave in May without anyone at the firm changing a line of code, because the provider changed the model underneath,” Dickson said. “A model version change should get the same scrutiny as any other production change.”

This article originally appeared on CIO.com.

item.title: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
item.description:
DeepSeek has been dealt a huge blow in the US, even as it continues to innovate and keep pace with, or in some cases outperform, rival models from American labs.

The US Secretary of Homeland Security has issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty, lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

Analyst Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, understands the concern. “When organizations use any type of hosted AI service, they’re potentially sending intellectual property, confidential business information, or other sensitive data into an environment where they may have very little visibility or control over what happens to it,” he said.

Government concerns

According to a document published in the US Federal Register, all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. will be banned from procurement by federal civilian agencies. This includes affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations.

Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice; it does not apply, however, to private consumers, the general public, state/local governments, or Department of Defense (DoD) national security systems.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” the Order stated. To begin with, the company’s servers are located in the People’ s Republic of China (PRC), whose legal system grants “extensive authority” to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private infrastructure.

DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users, the Order asserted. Its prompt response process may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC. This could give it “actionable intelligence” on US programs or individual users.

Further, the Order stated, DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that uncovered many iOS mobile apps with multiple critical vulnerabilities.

Until the ban takes full effect, DHS advised agencies to mitigate risk by monitoring inbound and outbound data traffic, implementing enhanced logging and controls on data exfiltration, and detecting and flagging anomalous activity.

Agencies can submit requests for exceptions to the ban in writing, and must provide a “compelling justification,” such as its impact on mission-critical functions, or other considerations related to national interest such as national security reviews, investigations, or security agreements, as reasons why such exemption should be granted,.

Security issues are rampant

The ban comes just as DeepSeek is open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house interference framework. DeepInfer powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with what the company said is high throughput and low latency. It features high-performance kernels, an optimized inference engine, structured outputs, and speculative decoding.

DeepSeek said its production token encoding and decoding components, which are aligned with processing logic behind the DeepSeek API, will bring the “same API behavior to community deployments.”

“Open models. Open kernels. Open inference,” DeepSeek posted to social media site X. “From private deployments to public clouds, we’ll keep working with the community to make large-scale inference more efficient.”

This isn’t its first roadblock from a cybersecurity perspective. Most notably, in January 2025, the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories, API secrets, and other sensitive information, through an unsecured database.

DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure, but it still raised questions about the overall security practices surrounding the platform, particularly for organizations considering entrusting it with their own sensitive business information, Avakian pointed out.

That’s not to imply that every DeepSeek model is “inherently malicious,” he said, but there are still major questions around data privacy, the potential for information access under Chinese laws, the security of the broader AI ecosystem, and the susceptibility of DeepSeek’s models to jailbreaks and manipulation.

“Taken together, [these issues] raise legitimate concerns about whether organizations can adequately understand and manage the risks involved,” Avakian said.

Enterprises should seriously assess associated risk

Enterprises are increasingly exploring DeepSeek, although most publicly-documented adoption has been in China, Avakian noted. Some DeepSeek models have also been made available through platforms like Microsoft Azure and AWS.

“There’s genuine enterprise interest in the technology, as organizations look for opportunities to improve productivity, offer new capabilities, or reduce costs,” Avakian said. Useful applications include document summarization, internal research, and coding assistance.

DeepInfer also has the potential to reduce costs, but possible benefits should be weighed against associated security risks, he pointed out. The framework was just released, so organizations are going to need to validate the claimed efficiencies in their own environments rather than assuming savings will automatically translate into lower operating costs.

He encouraged organizations to start with relatively low-risk use cases, preferably using “public, synthetic, or appropriately sanitized information,” within a sandboxed environment they control themselves.

The important question to ask: ‘What is the business problem we’re trying to solve?’ From there, Avakian said, determine whether DeepSeek is the best way to solve it, validate security controls, and expand the use cases based on risk tolerance. Effective governance and risk assessment are key, he noted: understand what you’re bringing into your environment, validate its security, restrict its permissions, and make sure you can monitor what it’s doing.

“Approach this like any other software supply chain decision,” Avakian advised. “The fact that something is open source, inexpensive, or technically impressive doesn’t automatically make it appropriate for enterprise use.”

Impact on the broader AI ecosystem

The fact that the Order also addressed third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations is important, Avakian said, because organizations may be using DeepSeek technologies indirectly, through vendors, software platforms, or other services, without necessarily knowing what’s operating underneath. “These are classic supply chain issues,” he observed.

It’s no longer enough to know which AI applications employees are using; enterprises must understand which models, frameworks, dependencies, and external services are embedded in products they’re purchasing and deploying, Avakian said. This means revisiting AI inventories, potentially updating procurement requirements, and expanding processes around third-party risk management, he advised.

“Ultimately, enterprises leveraging these tools need to understand not only the AI technologies they’re intentionally deploying, but also the technologies they’re inheriting through third parties,” he said.

This article originally appeared on CIO.com.

item.title: F5 rushes out emergency NGINX patches for three critical flaws
item.description:
F5 is once again disclosing cybersecurity flaws in its core offerings.

The app delivery and security provider has released out-of-band (OOB) security patches that address multiple flaws in NGINX, its high-performance software that controls digital traffic for websites. These include three critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to crash systems, execute code, and launch denial of service (DoS) attacks.

OOB security patches are emergency software updates released outside of normal maintenance cycles.

CVE-2026-15176, CVE-2026-97205, and CVE-2026-93479 are rated 9.2 in severity in the latest version (4.0) of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Impacted software products include NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager.

While F5 says it hasn’t discovered evidence that these issues are being exploited in the wild, it advises customers to install or upgrade to fixed versions. Analysts agree.

“NGINX is the front door: Reverse proxy, load balancer, and Kubernetes ingress,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, noting that transport layer security (TLS) usually terminates in NGINX. “Code execution on that box means seeing passwords, session cookies, and API tokens in the clear, plus the private keys that make it all trustworthy.”

Allowing attackers to crash systems

CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205 are ngx_http_core_module vulnerabilities in F5’s NGINX, which could cause a heap buffer overflow in the server’s worker process. This type of memory corruption could lead to a system crashing or restarting, thus giving attackers access. Threat actors could also execute code on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a technique intended to prevent exploitation by randomly arranging memory locations when an app starts, is disabled, or bypass ASLR altogether. The flaws could allow attackers to launch DoS attacks to make the server inaccessible to legitimate users, F5 explained.

CVE-2026-93479 is similar, in that it is a map directive flaw that could allow attackers to send crafted HTTP requests to cause a heap buffer overflow; they can also execute code when ASLR is disabled, or bypass it.

These vulnerabilities follow F5’s disclosure of CVE-2026-42530 in June. The flaw in ngx_http_v3_module in NGINX Open Source could also potentially allow remote attackers to cause DoS or trigger code execution.

Customers can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by avoiding use of the $request_filename variable and the alias directive in a location block, F5 said, and CVE-2026-97205 can be mitigated by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) and Server Side Includes (SSI).

Meanwhile, F5 advised mitigating CVE-2026-93479 by avoiding unnamed captures and instead using named captures and limiting their usage to the block with the regex match.

But, noted Seva Ioussoufovitch, senior research analyst at Infotech, “since NGINX is used across a wide swath of systems, this may increase the risk of service availability loss for many enterprises.”

The latest in a series of cybersecurity issues

While these three vulnerabilities are not known to be exploited in the wild, F5 has repeatedly borne the brunt of cyberattacks in recent years, which is troubling because the cybersecurity and app delivery networking (ADN) company serves tens of thousands of customers, including 80% of the Fortune 500, analysts noted.

Threat actors have repeatedly targeted flaws in its systems and products to map internal servers, hijack devices, breach systems, steal sensitive documents, and deploy data-wiping malware. Over the last five years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight actively-exploited F5 vulnerabilities; four of these have been targeted in ransomware attacks.

For instance, a 2025 nation-state breach and CISA’s Emergency Directive 26-01 centered on F5’s BIG-IP, and F5 said at the time that NGINX source code was not accessed. But, Dickson noted, NGINX’s own “warning shot” came in May when CVE-2026-42945, a rewrite module overflow nicknamed NGINX Rift, arrived with a public remote code execution proof of concept.

“This week’s alias and rewrite flaw lives in the same neighborhood,” he said, pointing out, “attackers read changelogs, too.”

Mitigation

Ioussoufovitch noted that the flaws are configuration-dependent, so enterprises should begin with an audit of current NGINX configurations to help risk-prioritize this patch. F5 also said that the risk of remote code execution (RCE) notably increases when ASLR is disabled, so users should double-check that ASLR and other typical OS-level protections are proactively enabled to at least limit the exploitation risk from similar types of attack.

Enterprises need to ensure they have a clear inventory of which of their systems are running NGINX, including those where it is embedded in other products. This is critical to supporting configuration audits, segmentation efforts, and NGINX worker monitoring efforts, which can indicate that attackers “are poking at these types of vulnerabilities,” Ioussoufovitch said.

“NGINX has already had multiple security releases this year, and I expect the trend to continue well into the future,” he noted.

Dickson agreed that inventorying is the first step. NGINX “hides inside” ingress controllers, appliances, and container images. Many teams get NGINX from their Linux distribution, not nginx.org, and Amazon Linux still lists the AIO fix as pending.

“A fix on the vendor’s site does not patch your servers,” he cautioned.

As well as performing the inventory, enterprises should search their configurations for aliases paired with rewrite, AIO paired with SSI, and map blocks using unnamed regex captures.

If an organization cannot patch today, the workarounds are simple, Dickson said: Disable AIO or stop serving SSI pages; switch map to named captures; confirm ASLR is on, run workers unprivileged; and segment the front door so it cannot reach the crown jewels. And, watch for worker processes that keep restarting.

“These flaws need the right configuration to bite, and that is the good news,” Dickson said. “The bad news is that many organizations may not know what their NGINX configurations actually say.”
